stories.title: Guinea-Bissau votes in referendum to rewrite constitution and boost presidential powers
stories.summary: Voters in military-ruled Guinea-Bissau, after a coup, vote on Sunday in a referendum to boost presidential powers before elections to restore civilian rule, a process mired in controversy. Voting got off to a slow start in some areas when the polling stations opened at 08:00 CET. According to media correspondents, security was stepped up at strategic points in the capital, with members of the National Guard and the police deployed at key locations. This referendum is taking place against a backdrop of political instability and is being challenged by the opposition, not only because it has already been approved and published in the Official Gazette of the Republic -before the people had been ‘heard’- but also because it was drafted by the military junta, that is, by a transitional government without prior consultation. "No one was consulted, neither political parties nor civil-society organisations, let alone traditional and religious leaders, and so on. So everything was done in secret," said the head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, Bubacar Turé, last week, speaking to Euronews. Turé also stressed that campaigners for a "no" vote in the referendum were not authorised to campaign. "This is not an environment of freedom," he added, which is another reason why the opposition has called for a boycott of today’s vote. Some analysts say the military government lacks legitimacy to change the constitution, which has fuelled discontent among citizens. "The fundamental question is: who drafted this constitution, and on whose behalf? To protect which interests or institutions? Who stands to gain from this constitution?" said Guinea-Bissau political analyst Paulino Quadé, speaking to the Associated Press.

stories.title: Serbia needs referendum on EU membership — former PM
stories.summary: Iceland’s citizens have opted to be free and refused from joining the European Union, Aleksandar Vulin said
article_sentences: BELGRADE, August 30.

Iceland’s citizens have opted to be free and refused from joining the European Union and Serbia should also hold a referendum on this matter, founder of Serbia’s Movement of Socialists and former Prime Minister Aleksandar Vulin said.
"Iceland has said ‘no’ to the European Union at the referendum.
They have opted to be free.
Neither threats no promises have helped - the Icelanders have made a decision on their own.
Why is no one asking the Serbs what they think about the EU’s blackmail and threats?
Why are Icelanders allowed to express their views on the EU, but Serbs are not?
When will a referendum on EU integration be held in Serbia?" he said, as quoted by his press service.
Iceland held a referendum on resuming negotiations on accessing the European Union on Saturday.

According to the latest updates cited by the RUV television company, 52% of voters opposed the idea, saying that this move will carry a risk of limiting Iceland’s sovereignty and imposing restrictions on fishing.
Iceland first applied for EU membership in 2009, but in 2013, a government skeptical of the EU halted the process.
Reykjavik is already part of the Schengen Area and the European Economic Area (EEA).

stories.title: France: Far-right and far-left lead polls
stories.summary: On April 18 and May 2 next year, France will vote to elect a new president to replace Emmanuel Macron. The outgoing president, who has served two terms, cannot run again, while the latest opinion polls are predicting a victory for Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally. Although the election is still more than seven months away, several potential candidates have already thrown their hats into the ring and announced their candidacies, including far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and former centre-right Prime Minister Édouard Philippe. But do any of them stand a chance of beating the far right? France 24 International Affairs editor Philip Turle shares further insights.
